newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: More ethnic Albanians on trial in Serbian court.
newsitem.headline: More ethnic Albanians on trial in Serbian court.

text.p: A group of ethnic Albanians stood trial on Tuesday in Pristina, capital of Serbia's troubled province of Kosovo, hours after the United States condemned a previous trial as seriously flawed.
The latest group was charged with participating in numerous "terrorist" actions in 1992-96, killing three Serbian policemen and one Serbian civilian, and trying to kill another 16 people.

Only three of the 15 members of the ethnic Albanian organisation Liberation Army of Kosovo, Besim Rama, Avni Nura and Idriz Aslani, are in custody while the others will be tried in absentia, the Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said.
The indictment said the defendants spent some time in Albania in 1992 training with the Albanian army for terrorist operations.

Tuesday's proceedings followed a trial last week also in Pristina that resulted in the imprisonment of 20 ethnic Albanians for alleged terrorism. The United States said that trial was marked by "serious irregularities".
The group, whose members received a total of 107 years in prison, was charged with association for the purpose of hostile activity, threatening territorial integrity, and terrorism.

"While the United States government is deeply concerned by acts of terrorism that have plagued Kosovo in recent months, the defendants' trial was marred by a number of serious judicial irregularities," the State Department said on Monday.

The Belgrade-based Humanitarian Law Fund also sharply criticised the trial, saying the prosecution failed to produce relevant evidence. It said torture was used to obtain confessions from the defendents.

The biggest ethnic Albanian party in Kosovo, the Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK), said Friday's long prison sentences "will be added to the numerous crimes committed so far against Albanians in Kosovo."
Kosovo, where ethnic Albanians outnumber Serbs nine to one, is widely regarded as a political powder keg which, if ignited, could wreck international peace efforts in the Balkans.

Some 30 people, both Serbs and Albanians, have been killed over the past year in guerrilla violence. Serbian police cracked down in the province in January, arresting some 70 people in a sweep following the guerrilla attacks.

The United States has made an improvement in Serbia's treatment of Kosovo one of its conditions for lifting remaining sanctions in force against federal Yugoslavia, which is comprised of Serbia and the tiny republic of Montenegro.
Serbia revoked Kosovo's autonomy in 1989, claiming its Albanian population wanted to secede and join neighbouring Albania.
The Albanians have boycotted Serbian institutions since but they have been warned by the United States that secession is not an option.
